_note: The Cubeon Friends mod's Minecraft version matrix, and the single source of
truth for it: mod/build.gradle reads this file to know what to compile
against, and cubeon/cubeonfriends.py reads it to pick which jar to install
into a profile. Two hand-maintained copies of the same table would drift,
and the failure mode of drift is a mod that loads into the wrong Minecraft.
There are exactly two brackets, and the line between them is not an API
change - it is a namespace change. Minecraft up to 1.21.x ships obfuscated,
so a Fabric mod's compiled references have to be in the *intermediary*
namespace (class_437.method_25411), which is what fabric-loom produces when
it remaps a build. Minecraft 26.x ships unobfuscated: its Fabric profile has
no intermediary library at all, and the names in the jar are already the real
ones. Fabric does no remapping at runtime, so no single jar can carry both
sets of references. Two jars is the floor, not a choice.
Within each bracket one jar covers everything, because the mod's source only
touches API that has not moved: Screen's lifecycle, addRenderableWidget, and
Button/EditBox/StringWidget (see the long comment in CubeonFriendsScreen for
why it never overrides render or an input callback). Intermediary names are
stable across versions by design, so the 1.20.1-built jar's references still
resolve on 1.21.x. tools/test_mod_compile.py is what keeps the source inside
that subset: the stub it compiles against deliberately omits everything that
changed shape between the two eras.
The newer bracket has no upper bound on purpose. Minecraft 26.2 or 26.3 will
almost certainly still have these widgets, and an open range means the button
keeps working on a version released after this launcher. If a future version
does rename something, the mixin is declared non-required, so the button goes
missing rather than the game.
Anything below 1.20.1 is deliberately absent: StringWidget and the Button
builder this screen is built from arrived around then, so there is no jar to
install and the launcher installs nothing rather than a mod that would crash
on class load.
compile_against is the OLDEST version in each bracket on purpose. A method
that exists in the oldest exists in the newer ones too; compiling against the
newest and running on the oldest is how you get a NoSuchMethodError.
mappings: 'official' pulls Mojang's own names via loom (these versions ship
obfuscated, and the source uses Mojang names). 'none' is for 26.x and later,
which ship unobfuscated - and because nothing has to be remapped, that jar
can be built with plain javac against the copy of Minecraft the launcher has
already downloaded, no Gradle and no network. See tools/build_mod_jars.py.
